vo: Our CIVIC Hack challenge is making municipal decisions easier to understand.
Toronto council decisions change streets every week, but the record is spread across agendas, staff reports and votes, and most residents only hear about a decision once it's made.
Take Sam, who rents on Eglinton Avenue East and works shifts.
To learn what happened to the two 59-storey towers proposed on their street, Sam would need a thirty-page staff report, this agenda page, and votes from two different meetings.
Here's the same thing with Text City Hall.
We're replaying the city's real records as they stood on July 8th, the day after North York Community Council met.
Sam texts the address. No app, no account, any phone.
It finds the ward in the city's own address data and lists the recent decisions there.
Sam replies 1.
On July 7th, community council passed an amendment six to nothing, but the motion to adopt the item lost, two to four.
No comment period is confirmed, so it says so. It never guesses a deadline from a meeting date.
Every reply links to the official record.
Sam texts WATCH.
On July 30th, City Council votes, and Sam gets two texts: Eglinton, amended twenty-five to one, and a Millwood Road rezoning in the same ward, amended twelve to eleven.
Reply 1 again, and Sam sees the outcome: City Council adopted it, with amendments.
Everything comes from City of Toronto open data and agenda pages. No AI writes the replies.
On two thousand real addresses, the ward lookup was never wrong.
Working today: the full conversation, in the browser, with real records. Not built yet: a real phone number and live alerts.
Council is between terms after the election, so nothing is open for comment. The demo replays past dates, clearly labelled.
To pilot it, a city needs a text number connected to this code, a nightly data refresh, and staff to review the wording.
It costs a few cents per conversation, and any city with open council data can adapt it.
The goal: residents hear about decisions while they can still have a say.
Try it at ripasso.github.io/civichacks.
